<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is a full-stack application for a voice-interactive AI companion with a Live2D avatar. It combines real-time voice and visual interaction, multiple LLM/ASR/TTS implementations, and a customizable user interface (both web and desktop). Here’s how to design an accurate system design diagram for Open-LLM-VTuber:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Backend Server & API: Centralized server entry point (e.g. run_server.py, routes.py, websocket_handler.py) that handles incoming HTTP and WebSocket requests.
   • Agent & Inference Modules: Under “src/open_llm_vtuber/agent” – these include various LLM providers (OpenAI, Claude, etc.), basic memory, stateless agents, and the agent factory. They orchestrate conversation state and query the LLM components.
   • ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition): Found inside “src/open_llm_vtuber/asr” which includes multiple implementations (e.g. azure_asr, whisper_cpp_asr, sherpa_onnx_asr, etc.). This component converts input speech into text.
   • TTS (Text-to-Speech): In “src/open_llm_vtuber/tts”, which contains several TTS options (azure_tts, bark_tts, gpt_sovits_tts, etc.), converting generated text into audio output.
   • VAD (Voice Activity Detection): In “src/open_llm_vtuber/vad”, responsible for detecting when the user is speaking.
   • Conversation & Chat Management: Modules under “src/open_llm_vtuber/conversations” and “src/open_llm_vtuber/chat_history_manager.py” that manage multi-turn dialogues and persistent chat logs.
   • Live2D Integration: The Live2D models (in “live2d-models” and “assets”) and configuration for the Live2D avatar by “src/open_llm_vtuber/live2d_model.py”. This ties the visual expressions, movements, and sound responses to the backend decisions.
   • Configuration Manager: Under “src/open_llm_vtuber/config_manager” along with “config_templates” provides all customizable settings for agents, ASR/TTS, characters, and more.
   • Frontend Client: The “frontend” directory and “web_tool” indicate that there is a web-based UI available to interact with the AI companion. This UI likely communicates with the backend server via HTTP or WebSocket.
   • Utilities & Support Components: Additional modules for translation (“src/open_llm_vtuber/translate”), media streaming (“src/open_llm_vtuber/utils/stream_audio.py”), and overall service context.

2. Define the Relationships and Interactions:
   • The Frontend (web and/or desktop client) sends user input (voice, text, UI actions) to the Backend Server.
   • The Backend Server routes the incoming data to the Conversation Manager, which then further dispatches the data to the Agent module if a response from an LLM is needed.
   • For voice input, the data first passes through the ASR module (after possible VAD pre-processing) to convert audio to text.
   • The Agent, depending on the mode (memory-based or stateless), sends the text to the appropriate LLM interface (such as OpenAI-compatible or local LLM implementations).
   • The resulting textual AI response is forwarded to the TTS module to generate an audio response.
   • The Live2D component receives instructions (e.g., corresponding expressions, motions, or lip-sync data) and uses the pre-configured models from “live2d-models” to visually realize the avatar’s reaction.
   • Configuration Manager acts as a central dynamic repository for settings that configure every module (agents, asr, tts, etc.).
   • Additionally, persistent storage (chat logs) maintains conversation history, enabling session restoration.

3. Emphasize Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Modular architecture: Each module (ASR, TTS, Agent, VAD, etc.) is encapsulated within its own directory with interchangeable implementations following defined interfaces.
   • Factory patterns: For creating agents, LLMs, and translating between various module types (as seen in agent_factory.py, asr_factory.py, tts_factory.py, etc.).
   • Pluggability and configuration-driven design: The configuration files (in config_templates and config_manager) allow switching between different underlying technologies with minimal code changes.
   • Separation of concerns: Clear distinction between data processing (ASR/TTS), AI inference (Agent and LLM modules), and UI/interaction handling (web_tool and frontend).

4. Include Relevant Technologies & Frameworks:
   • Backend: Likely built with Python (based on the .py structure and pyproject.toml for dependency management).
   • Frontend: JavaScript-based (as seen with index.html, main.js, recorder.js in the web_tool) as well as a desktop client implementation.
   • Live2D: Integration of Live2D Cubism models for avatar depiction.
   • External APIs: Support for cloud-based ASR/TTS and various LLM providers (Azure ASR, OpenAI, etc.).
   • CI/CD: GitHub workflows for code analysis and scanning indicating integration with tools like CodeQL and Ruff.

5. Tailoring the Diagram for this Project Type:
   • Since it’s a full-stack application combining real-time voice and visual processing, emphasize clear separation between:
       – Client-side (Frontend/desktop client)
       – Server-side Components (API Gateway, Conversation & Agent management)
       – Functional Modules (ASR, LLM, TTS, VAD, Live2D)
   • Highlight the configuration and customization pathways that let developers easily swap or update components.
   • Show integration or dependency flows (e.g., the ASR module receiving audio from the client, then feeding text to the agent, and similarly for TTS).

6. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Draw nodes for each major component:
       - Frontend Client (Web & Desktop)
       - API & Web Server (handles HTTP/WebSocket requests)
       - Conversation Manager (chat history, conversation routing)
       - Agent System (including agent interface, factories, and different LLM implementations)
       - ASR Module (with multiple implementations shown, possibly in a sub-group)
       - TTS Module (with branch icons for different TTS providers)
       - VAD Module
       - Live2D Avatar Engine (with related assets/resources)
       - Configuration Manager (central configuration repository)
   • Use directional arrows to denote data flow between:
       - Client → Server → Conversation Manager → Agent Module
       - Agent → LLM Provider(s)
       - Server/Agent → ASR (for incoming audio) and TTS (for outgoing audio)
       - Server → Live2D component (to trigger avatar animations and expressions)
   • Label each component clearly and consider using color coding or different shapes (e.g., rectangles for services, cylinders for persistent storage, and clouds for external APIs).
   • Optionally include auxiliary components:
       - External dependencies (like GPU/cloud APIs)
       - CI/CD pipeline (GitHub workflows) as a supporting background process if necessary

7. Be Detailed, Yet Organized:
   • Don’t shy away from splitting the diagram into layers or sub-systems to capture complexity.
   • Ensure callouts for configuration-driven decisions and modularity patterns (like factories or interfaces), which are critical to understanding how new modules can be integrated.

In summary, when the principal software engineer creates the diagram, it should clearly map out the high-level flow from the user’s voice and visual inputs to backend processing (conversion via ASR, LLM-based conversation management, TTS for output) and finally to the avatar’s dynamic display via Live2D. The design should highlight the plug-and-play modular components, the clear separation of frontend and backend responsibilities, and the multiple configurations managed by the system. This robust visualization will be invaluable for both code comprehension and future system expansion.
</explanation>
